records.place: Rizes, near Tripoli, Mantinia PDO, Arcadia, Peloponnese, Greece

wine.name: Mantinia
wine.grapes: Moschofilero alone, the pink skinned grape of the plateau.
wine.sites: Selected vineyards around the villages of Rizes, Lithovounia and Agiorgitika, at about 680 metres on the south eastern side of the Mantinia plateau, below the foothills of Mount Parnon.
wine.making: The grapes are given a short cold soak on their skins, about eight hours at 10 degrees Celsius, before a slow, cool fermentation. The wine then rests only briefly in stainless steel tanks on its fine lees before it is bottled young, with no oak.
wine.glass: Rose petal, lemon blossom and lime peel with a touch of white pepper and fresh ginger; light in body and low in alcohol, with bright, almost tart acidity and a clean, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first two or three years, while the perfume is fresh; a good vintage holds a little longer.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of modest size.

label.means: The protected appellation of the high Arcadian plateau, white and sparkling, at least 85 per cent Moschofilero.
The grape: pink skinned and aromatic, pressed pale into a white wine.
Tselepos Estate in Greek, the name the family's wines carry at home.

records.table: Domaine Tselepos makes its Mantinia from Moschofilero grown at Rizes and two neighbouring villages, high on the Arcadian plateau. Given a few hours on the skins and bottled young from steel, it smells of rose and lemon blossom and drinks light, dry and bright.
records.story: The house began with an oenologist trained in Dijon who came to Arcadia in 1981 to advise the growers of the Mantinia plateau, an appellation drawn up only ten years before. In 1989, by the house's own account, he and his wife founded their own estate outside the village of Rizes, on the clay hills at the foot of Mount Parnon, at the south eastern edge of the plateau. Their first Mantinia under the family name followed within a year or two, Moschofilero bottled alone. The estate's own timeline then runs on through a red blend in 1993, its own winery opened in 1994, and in 1996 Amalia Brut, a sparkling Moschofilero made by the traditional method of Champagne, which the house counts as the first sparkling Moschofilero made that way. The family later took on Driopi, an estate in Nemea, and a cellar on Santorini, so its three wineries cover three of the Greek appellations a candidate meets. Through all of it the Mantinia has stayed the house's calling card: Moschofilero picked late on the cold plateau and bottled as a pure, fresh dry white. For a sommelier it shows what the appellation is meant to be: perfume, freshness and low alcohol from a cold, high place.

others.name: Amalia Brut

Moschofilero smells like Muscat but is not a Muscat, and Mantinia is dry.
Driopi is the family's Nemea estate, red Agiorgitiko, not a Mantinia wine.

records.place: Artemisio, Mantinia PDO, Arcadia, Peloponnese, Greece

wine.name: Mantinia
wine.grapes: Moschofilero alone, from the family's own organically farmed vines.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards in three zones of the plateau, Artemisio, Zevgolatio and Agiorgitika, at about 627 to 655 metres, mostly planted with Moschofilero.
wine.making: Made only from the estate's organically grown grapes, the wine is fermented in stainless steel at a cool temperature to keep the grape's perfume, with no oak, and bottled young.
wine.glass: Orange blossom, rose and lemon zest with a hint of lychee; light and dry, with crisp acidity and a short, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Made to be drunk in its first two or three years, while the scent of orange blossom is fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of modest size.

label.means: The protected appellation of the Arcadian plateau, at least 85 per cent Moschofilero.
Spiropoulos Estate in Greek, the house's name on its home labels.

records.table: Domaine Spiropoulos is one of the plateau's old families and an early organic grower, and its Mantinia is Moschofilero from its own vines around Artemisio, fermented cool in steel. It smells of orange blossom and rose, light and dry, a clean aperitif.
records.story: The Spiropoulos family has tended vines on the Mantinia plateau since 1860, by its own account, near the ruins of ancient Mantineia in the heart of Arcadia. For more than a century its wine was a farm's wine, made for the household and the district. The modern estate took shape when the family began a new winery in 1989, built around a traditional Arcadian stone tower, and from it bottled Moschofilero under its own name in the Mantinia appellation, drawn up in 1971. The family turned early to organic farming: by the account of Wines of Greece its vineyards met the European organic rules from 1993 and were certified by the Greek body DIO in 1996. The family later added an estate in Nemea for red Agiorgitiko, and it makes a sparkling Moschofilero, Ode Panos, beside its Mantinia. The Mantinia remains the wine the house is known by: organic Moschofilero from three zones of the plateau, fermented cool and bottled young. For a sommelier it is the traditional, unadorned face of the appellation, and a natural pour for a guest who asks for an organic Greek white.

records.place: Fteri, Mantinia PDO, Arcadia, Peloponnese, Greece

wine.name: Holy Mania
wine.sites: The family's own low yielding vineyards in the Fteri area at the centre of the plateau, at about 640 metres.
wine.making: The house works with as little intervention and as few additions as it can: the Moschofilero is fermented wild, with the yeasts of the vineyard and cellar rather than a chosen strain, and the wine is bottled young.
wine.glass: White peach, citron and rose with a note of jasmine on the finish; dry and light in body, with fresh acidity and a little more texture than the house's Fteri.
wine.ageing: Drinks well on release and keeps for at least three years, by the house's account.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The wine's name, a play on Mantinia, the appellation it carries.
The protected appellation of the Arcadian plateau, at least 85 per cent Moschofilero.
The family's winery at Fteri, in the centre of the plateau.

records.table: Holy Mania is the Mantinia of Troupis, a family winery at Fteri in the centre of the plateau: Moschofilero from its own vines, fermented with wild yeasts. White peach, citron and jasmine, dry and fresh; serve it cool, not icy.
records.story: The Troupis family has worked the land of the Mantinia plateau, an appellation since 1971, from the 1970s on, growing vines and fruit and, by its own account, making wine for the household each year and selling the rest of its grapes. In 2010 the family chose to build on its own vineyards rather than sell their fruit, and the winery was set up at Fteri, in the middle of the plateau at about 700 metres. The same year it launched its first labels under the name of the village, Fteri, and its first exports were Fteri Moschofilero, a wine labelled PGI Arcadia. The winery has kept planting its own vines year by year and has trialled Moschofilero on different rootstocks, along with small batches of forgotten local grapes such as Kolliniatiko. Holy Mania is its Mantinia, the house's wine that carries the appellation: Moschofilero from the family's own vines around Fteri, fermented wild with the yeasts of the place. Beside it the house makes Hoof and Lur, a skin contact Moschofilero, and a sweet wine. For a sommelier the house shows the plateau's younger generation: small, family run, curious, and built on the one local grape.

records.place: Steno, Mantinia PDO, Arcadia, Peloponnese, Greece

wine.name: Mantinia
wine.sites: The family's dry farmed vineyards on clay loam around Steno, Lithovounia and Agiorgitika, at about 670 to 700 metres.
wine.making: The Moschofilero is given a short cold soak and fermented cool in stainless steel, then rested on its fine lees with stirring before it is bottled, with no oak.
wine.glass: Rose petal, lemon and grapefruit with white pepper and a hint of green apple; light, dry and lively, with crisp acidity and a touch of texture from the lees.

records.table: Bosinakis is a family winery at Steno on the Mantinia plateau that works with Moschofilero alone, and its Mantinia, first bottled in 2009, comes from dry farmed vines at about 700 metres. Rose, lemon and white pepper, light and crisp.
records.story: The Bosinakis family's winery at Steno, a village of the Mantinia plateau south of Tripoli, began making wine in 1992, and for its first years it did not bottle under its own name. That changed in 2009, when a brother and sister of the family released their first wine under the Bosinakis label, a Mantinia from Moschofilero. For some years it was the one label they made. The family's vines lie around Steno and the neighbouring villages of Lithovounia and Agiorgitika, on clay loam at about 700 metres, and they are dry farmed, as the cold, wet winters of the plateau allow. The range has since grown by small steps, all of it from the one grape: a rosé, Iereia, from the pink skins of Moschofilero, and an orange wine, Aspela, given weeks on its skins. The family's line runs back beyond the winery, but the sources disagree on how far, and the record does not guess. Mantinia's wine was already sent to Athens in the nineteenth century, by the account of Wines of Greece; houses like this one bottle it at the village. For a sommelier Bosinakis is the appellation from one family's vines, a small house known at home and in a few export markets.

wine.name: Mantinia Nassiakos
wine.sites: The house's vineyard at Zevgolatio, on the Mantinia plateau, at about 650 metres.
wine.making: The Moschofilero is pressed at the Nassiakos winery in Mantinia and fermented slowly at a steady 17 to 18 degrees Celsius in stainless steel, to hold the grape's perfume, then bottled young with no oak.

records.table: Semeli Mantinia Nassiakos is the Moschofilero of a house better known for Nemea, made at its Nassiakos winery in Mantinia from vines at Zevgolatio. Fermented slowly in steel, it is all lemon and rose petal, light and crisp.
records.story: Semeli began in 1979 at Stamata, in the hills of Attica north of Athens, where its first winery was built, and it took its name from Semele, the mother of Dionysus in Greek myth. From there the company bought vineyards in the Peloponnese, in Nemea and on the Mantinia plateau. In 2003 it opened a large modern winery at Koutsi, at about 600 metres in Nemea, among its own vines, and that cellar became the heart of the house, making the house's Agiorgitiko. Its third winery is in Mantinia: the Nassiakos winery, which by the house's account had made Moschofilero for some forty years when it joined Semeli. The house's Mantinia carries that cellar's name, Nassiakos, on its label, and comes from Moschofilero grown at Zevgolatio at about 650 metres, fermented slowly and cool. A house whose reds come from Nemea and whose white comes from the plateau above Tripoli holds the two Peloponnese appellations a candidate meets most often under one name. For a sommelier the wine shows how a larger house keeps a separate cellar on the plateau for its Moschofilero.
